This cycle established two new results in the catalog's Cusick thread
(`CusickShiftThreeDensity.lean`, `CusickPeriodicity.lean`):

* **Exact density for the first `s₂(t) = 2` shift:** `c_3 = 11/16`, with the
  explicit Cusick bound `1/2 + 2^{-(2·2+1)} = 17/32` cleared by a margin of `5/32`;
  propagated to the doubling orbit `{3, 6, 12, …}`.
* **General pure periodicity:** for every `t ≥ 1`, the Cusick predicate
  `P_t(n) := s₂(n) ≤ s₂(n+t)` is purely periodic in `n` with period
  `2^{L + s₂(t)}` (`t < 2^L`), so `c_t` is a dyadic rational equal to
  `cusickCount t (2^{L+s₂(t)}) / 2^{L+s₂(t)}`.

These suggest the following bold, testable conjectures.

## C1. Exact period is `2^{(length t) + s₂(t)}` (minimality)

The proved theorem gives `2^{L+s₂(t)}` as *a* period for any `L > log₂ t`. The data
(`t ≤ 31`) shows the *minimal* period is exactly `2^{(length t) + s₂(t)}` with
`length t = ⌊log₂ t⌋ + 1`.

*The key insight is* that the upper `s₂(t)` carry-positions are the only high bits
that can ever influence the predicate, so the minimal period is forced to be no
smaller than `2^{length t + s₂(t)}` by exhibiting two residues differing only in
bit `length t + s₂(t) − 1` whose predicate values disagree.

*Why now?* The periodicity theorem already isolates `L + s₂(t)` as the operative
exponent; closing the gap to *minimality* only requires a single explicit
distinguishing residue, which the carry analysis in `overflow_false` now makes
constructible.

## C2. Closed form for the numerator `c_t · 2^{L+s₂(t)}`

Define `A(t) := cusickCount t (2^{L+s₂(t)})`. The proved rationality makes `A(t)` a
well-defined integer; measured values are `A(1)=3, A(3)=11, A(7)=43, A(15)=171,
A(31)=683`, i.e. `A(2^k−1) = (2·4^k+1)/3`.

*The key insight is* that for `t = 2^k − 1` (a block of `k` ones) the carry automaton
is a single counter, so `A(t)` satisfies a linear recurrence `A_{k+1} = 4A_k − 1`,
giving the closed form `(2·4^k+1)/3`.

*Why now?* With periodicity proven, `A(t)` is a finite, computable integer for each
`t`; the recurrence can be checked exactly in Lean for the all-ones family by the
same digit-concatenation lemma used for `t = 3`.

## C3. Monotone bias: `c_t − 1/2 ≥ 2^{-2 s₂(t)}` for all `t` (strengthening)

Cusick's bound is `c_t − 1/2 ≥ 2^{-(2 s₂(t)+1)}`. Every measured value beats *twice*
that: `c_t − 1/2 ≥ 2^{-2 s₂(t)}` (e.g. `t=3`: `3/16 ≥ 1/16`; `t=7`: `11/64 ≥ 1/64`).

*The key insight is* that the overflow regime contributes a *deterministic* deficit
of one full digit (`s₂(n+t) ≤ s₂(n) − 1`), which over-counts the trivial `1/2` bias
by a factor of two relative to the conjectured slack.

*Why now?* The `overflow_false` lemma already proves the one-digit deficit pointwise;
turning it into the doubled bias only needs a counting comparison over a single
period, now that the period is finite and explicit.

## C4. Density depends only on the odd part *and* the digit pattern

The catalog's doubling invariance shows `c_t` depends only on `odd(t)`. Data shows a
finer rule: `c_t` depends only on the *cyclic-free binary pattern* of `odd(t)`
(e.g. `c_3 = c_9 = 11/16`, both odd parts `3` and `9 = 1001` sharing pattern
structure).

*The key insight is* that the carry automaton reads `t`'s bits as transition labels,
so two shifts with conjugate label sequences induce isomorphic automata and hence
equal stationary densities.

*Why now?* The periodic-count formula `c_t = A(t)/2^{L+s₂(t)}` reduces the
conjecture to an equality of two explicitly computable integers, checkable per pair.

## C5. Effective convergence rate for `c_t`

Since `P_t` is periodic with period `p = 2^{L+s₂(t)}`, the finite densities converge
*exactly* on aligned windows: `|(1/N)#{n<N : P_t(n)} − c_t| ≤ p/N`.

*The key insight is* that periodicity upgrades the *asymptotic* density to a finite
window identity, so the error is purely the boundary term of one incomplete period.

*Why now?* `cusickCount_period` already gives the exact value on aligned windows;
the remaining bound is the elementary estimate on the at-most-`p` leftover indices.

For n=3, explicitly characterize all cliques in the 1-skeleton and verify they correspond to faces. For n=4, construct a specific 4-clique in the 1-skeleton that is not the vertex set of any face, using the fact that two permutation matrices are adjacent in B_n iff the corresponding permutations differ by a single transposition. concept.lean_guess: For n <= 2, B_n is respectively a point or a segment, so the clique-face property is immediate. For n = 3, two permutation vertices are adjacent exactly when their quotient permutation has a single nontrivial cycle; every nonidentity element of S_3 has this property, so the 1-skeleton of B_3 is complete on six vertices. However B_3 is 4-dimensional and its facets are given by equations x_ij = 0, each containing only four permutation vertices, so a five-vertex clique is not the vertex set of any face. Thus B_3 fails the property. For n >= 3, B_n contains a face isomorphic to B_3 by fixing n-3 rows and columns to the corresponding identity entries. Since the clique-face property passes to faces, B_n also fails it.

combinatorial model used in `Skeleton.lean` / `CliqueFace.lean`.

* 1-skeleton (Brualdi–Gibson): `σ ~ τ` iff `σ⁻¹ τ` is a single cycle.
* Face vertex sets (Billera–Sarangarajan): `S` is a face vertex set iff every permutation
  whose graph lies in the union of the graphs of `S` already belongs to `S`.

## 1. Small cases

### n = 1
* 1 vertex (`id`). Skeleton: no edges. Cliques: `∅, {id}`.
* `cellUnion {id} = {(0,0)}`; the only permutation supported there is `id`. Both cliques are
  face vertex sets. **Property holds.**

### n = 2
* 2 vertices: `id`, `(0 1)`. Their graphs `{(0,0),(1,1)}` and `{(0,1),(1,0)}` are **disjoint**.
* Skeleton = `K_2` (one edge, since `(0 1)` is a single cycle).
* Every subset is a face vertex set, because disjoint graphs force any permutation supported
  on `cellUnion S` to coincide with a member of `S`. **Property holds.**

### n = 3
* 6 vertices. Every non-identity element of `S_3` is a transposition or a 3-cycle — all single
  cycles — so the skeleton is the **complete graph `K_6`**: every subset is a clique.
* Counterexample clique: the three transpositions `(0 1), (0 2), (1 2)`.
  * support union (`cellUnion`):
    | from\to | 0 | 1 | 2 |
    |---|---|---|---|
    | 0 | • | • | • |
    | 1 | • | • | • |
    | 2 | • | • | • |

    All 9 cells are occupied (each diagonal cell `(i,i)` is fixed by one of the transpositions;
    each off-diagonal cell is realised by the transposition swapping those coordinates).
  * Hence **every** permutation of `Fin 3` is supported on the union; in particular the 3-cycle

clique-face property iff `n ≤ 2`; the mechanism is the disjoint-graph dichotomy and the
three-transposition counterexample for `n ≥ 3`).

## Conjecture 1 — Exact count of "bad" cliques in `B_n`
For `n ≥ 3`, count the cliques of the 1-skeleton that are **not** face vertex sets, as a
function of `n`. Conjecture: this count grows super-exponentially and admits a clean formula in
terms of subsets of permutations whose support union strictly contains them.
*The key insight is...* a clique fails to be a face exactly when its support union admits a
permutation outside the clique, so "bad cliques" are counted by support patterns with extra
perfect matchings.
*Why now?* We have a verified combinatorial characterisation (`IsFaceVertexSet` via support
closure) that turns the geometric question into a finite enumeration amenable to `decide`.

## Conjecture 2 — Minimal bad clique size
For `n ≥ 3`, the smallest clique that is not a face vertex set has size exactly `3`, realised by
three transpositions, and never smaller.
*The key insight is...* size-2 cliques are edges, and edges are always faces of the Birkhoff
polytope (Brualdi–Gibson), so the first obstruction can only appear at size `3`.
*Why now?* `not_cliqueFace_fin_of_three` already exhibits a size-3 witness; proving minimality
needs only that all 2-element cliques satisfy `IsFaceVertexSet`, a finite local check.

## Conjecture 3 — Clique-face property for other transportation polytopes
Replace `B_n` by the transportation polytope of nonnegative matrices with prescribed row/column
sums `(r, c)`. Conjecture: the clique-face property holds iff the bipartite support graph forced
by `(r, c)` has no induced structure realising three pairwise-adjacent vertices with full
support — generalising the `n ≤ 2` threshold.
*The key insight is...* the disjoint-graph dichotomy is really a statement about when distinct
vertices can share a support cell, which is governed by the margins `(r, c)`.
*Why now?* Mathlib's `doublyStochastic` development gives the `r = c = 1` case; the support-union
face model ports directly to general margins.

## Conjecture 4 — Graph-theoretic identity of the failing instances
For `n ≥ 3`, the 1-skeleton of `B_n` restricted to any "support-saturated" set of permutations
is a complete multipartite graph, and the clique-face failures are exactly its non-maximal
cliques.
*The key insight is...* adjacency is "differ by a single cycle", and saturating the support
makes single-cycle differences ubiquitous, pushing the skeleton toward completeness (already
`K_6` for `n = 3`).
*Why now?* We proved the `n = 3` skeleton is complete; the multipartite refinement is the
natural next falsifiable step with the same `Equiv.Perm.IsCycle` toolkit.

## Conjecture 5 — Stability of the threshold under symmetry quotients
Quotient `B_n` by a cyclic symmetry of the index set. Conjecture: the clique-face threshold
remains `n ≤ 2` for the quotient polytope, i.e. the obstruction is symmetry-robust.
*The key insight is...* the three-transposition obstruction uses only three coordinates, so it
survives any symmetry that does not collapse `{0,1,2}`.
*Why now?* The counterexample is local (three points), making it an ideal probe for robustness
under group actions encoded with `Equiv.Perm` conjugation already in scope.
